title: How do you feel about European cinema other than British and French cinema?

commenti.body: I see no point in grouping films by nationality and trying to form blanket judgments about those groups. Good films get made in all parts of Europe. It really depends on the filmmaker, and the particular film. And nationality is a fairly weak connective trait. A Swedish film could easily have more in common with an Italian or Polish film than it does with any other Swedish film. Etc.

> It seems like most European countries are unpopular with film lovers, which is weird.

Not sure I see that. You exclude France and England, but many European countries have an extremely strong film history. Italy is pretty much a guaranteed Top 4 or 5 film country of all time behind USA, Japan, and France. Germany has an extremely strong film history. Poland has produced some massive filmmakers, as has Greece and Spain and Czech. And are we including Russia in there?

These countries may be close in proximity, but their industries and films are unique to their own countries and can't all be grouped as "European cinema" as if it were a monolith.

Watched a lot of German movies this year. Highly recommend Aguirre, wrath of god, Fitzcarraldo, run Lola run, downfall and Querelle. All very different movies too. However all quiet on the western front (2023). Cannot recommend that one. 

Also great films can come from anywhere that much is abundantly clear to me

Also, I don’t know what film circles you are frequenting where European cinema isn’t popular. Even though Hollywood is still the hegemony (for better or for worse) of the film industry/popular cinema, European cinema is still in heavy contention for the most popular kind of cinema tbh.

I think Czechia/Czechoslovakia is the most underrated country for cinema. They had an interesting combination of a really robust state supported film industry because they were a communist country but also (at least for a few years in the 60s) very little censorship. A lot of these movies don’t have much of a critical reputation because they never played in the west and have only been available since the 90s but there’s some truly incredible movies there. Some favorites are:

-The Cremator and anything else by Juraj Herz
-Daisies
-Invention For Destruction
-Alice
-Marketa Lazarova
-Intimate Lighting
-Witchhammer
-Birds, Orphans, and Fools

I could go on, there’s so many amazing ones.

> It seems like most European countries are unpopular with film lovers, which is weird.

I'm not sure this is true. How many names in film history are more canonical among cinephiles than Ingmar Bergman, Federic Fellini, Werner Herzog, Andrei Tarkovsky, Fritz Lang, Carl Theodore Dreyer, Michelangelo Antonionior, Roman Polanski or Sergio Leone? Beyond those obvious canonical names, there is a long list of continental European filmmakers with serious cult followings in the English-speaking world: Pedro Almodovar, Paul Verhoeven, Jean-Pierre Melville, Krzysztof Kieślowski, etc.

>Do you have a favourite country from Europe for films other than Britain or France?

I'm not sure I have a favorite, per se, but I enjoy quite a few German, Italian and Spanish films. But I think most European countries have been the site of great filmmaking.

>Do you usually use streaming services to get films from the country?

I use the Criterion Channel, which has an incredible collection of films from different countries and time periods.

I have to strongly disagree with your asserted premise. 

On the contrary, you'll find that most cinephiles gravitate towards European arthouse cinema because it encompasses such a varied pantheon of auteurs, be it Bergman (Sweden), Fellini (Italy), Tarr (Hungary), Almodovar (Spain), Murnau (Germany), Lang (Austria), etc. 

Europe has a very rich cultural and artistic heritage, and perhaps even more importantly, has shown a capacity to adapt and re-invent itself in several artforms relative to the social and economic situations each of its countries has found itself in. Both German Expressionism and Italian Neorealism, for example, were born as reactions to the cultural shifts of the time and the lack of financial means which forced their creatives to experiment more. 

Bearing that in mind, I assume your question comes from the oft-stated importance of the French New Wave, as well as the great English epics of someone like Lean, so to answer your question directly, I think that Europe as a whole has contributed immensely to cinema as an art form, so much so that American cinema is often (perhaps unjustly, given its artistic contributions) viewed as "entertainment" as opposed to the more "artistic" cinema of Europe, which has also its fair share of populist films (e.g., "cinéma populaire" in France). 

If you have some nearby, art house cinemas are a great place to discover new films, otherwise TCM, the Criterion Collection and MUBI.
I completely agree. National categorization doesn't make sense for an art form that is so global. Influences don't travel, like they did and do with other art forms. Influences are direct in cinema.
And of course two-time Best Picture/Best Director winner Miloš Forman.
